sm: Mike Mazza of the Ayn Rand Institute talks with Stefan Guillard, a philosophy of science PhD student at Radboud University in the Netherlands, who founded the Journal of Trial and Error. Stefan explains that the idea began in 2018 after a lecture on open access, when he and others noted that science leaves out things like negative and null results. The journal launched in 2020 and is meant to publish failed experiments and interesting methodological failures. He uses nudging as an example: published studies showed large effects, but a meta study that gathered unpublished null results found only small to medium effects. He also cites German chemists whose machine learning model, trained on published reactions, predicted yields far too high until it was retrained on their own lab data.

Stefan describes why negative results go unpublished as a vicious cycle. Journals tend to reject them, scientists know that, and under time pressure they write up positive results first. Researchers also fear that a list of null results will hurt their careers, though Stefan pitches a publication as still a publication. He says many regular journals now invite negative results, yet their output remains ninety to ninety-five percent positive. On why it matters, he says knowing how the world does not work is itself a scientific insight, and decisions rest on evidence. He gives intermittent fasting as an example: his journal published a study finding no mental health benefit, and he heard of other unpublished ones, so the literature may overstate how often it works.

Stefan links the problem to the replication crisis. If a false hypothesis is tested twenty times, one study will find an effect by chance, and if only that one is published, replications will fail. He adds that knowing positive results are favored pushes some scientists toward questionable practices, such as rerunning analyses or redefining outliers, which can shade into fraud. Mike asks whether the problem is mainly in pure research, compared with building technology where repeated failure is expected. Stefan says applied fields have it too and returns to the chemistry case, where the machine learning model became accurate once trained on lab data that included low-yield reactions. Mike then raises private-sector motives for keeping failures quiet.

Mike continues on commercial motives. Stefan says intellectual property may be a factor, since publishing failures could count as prior art, and competition worries are real. Even so, people at companies tell him it is frustrating when academic findings they rely on turn out not to work. He adds that companies lose knowledge internally, because failures from twenty or thirty years ago were poorly documented, and newcomers are told not to try something that might now work with new technology. Mike asks whether scientists really neglect error, since science is adversarial and replication tries to refute claims. Stefan says scientists claim that philosophy, but in practice there were few replications before the replication crisis. Big, high-stakes refutations get published, while mundane null results do not.

Mike asks whether the problem is sociological, with individual scientists valuing errors but the incentive structures not rewarding them. Stefan agrees, noting shame and the fact that scientists who disprove their own results often do not go public, or are rejected when they do. He says some scientists wrongly think their dead ends interest no one, such as months spent optimizing temperature that get two sentences in a thesis chapter. Other researchers would want to know which conditions were wrong. Mike lists different kinds of error, such as recording mistakes, flawless studies that contradict the hypothesis, and wrong or inapplicable methods. Stefan says his journal publishes two types: flawlessly executed research that gives an unexpected result, and interesting methodological mistakes.

Stefan says the first type needs careful interpretation, because absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, but it is still good data that regular journals reject as not interesting enough. For the second type, the journal asks whether the failure could reasonably have been foreseen and whether other scientists might end up at the same dead end. He tells of a PhD student who spent two years on something that did not work, then learned at a conference that everyone already knew, though it was not in the literature. Asked how he thinks of these results, he says he calls it failure: a goal was set and not reached, even when nothing blameworthy happened. Mike objects that error implies a mistake, and that a rigorous study contradicting a well-founded hypothesis is not one.

Stefan says failing does not require blame, but many people hear failure as blameworthy. He argues that swapping the word does not help, because the negative connotation attaches to the phenomenon and the new word picks it up. Asked where the shame comes from, he points to impostor syndrome in academia and the irrational thought that better thinking would have avoided the dead end. Scientists say they like the initiative but often say they will not send anything in themselves. Mike suggests that scientists could publish earlier failed attempts alongside a positive result, as with early rocket crashes before success. Stefan says the journal's main aim was to open up discussion of publishing such results and to provide a dedicated, memorable platform.

Stefan says the journal's goal is to become unnecessary once regular journals embrace these results. He urges scientists short on time to put detailed accounts of failures into supplementary files, longer than a sentence like we optimized for temperature. On publishing versus sharing, he says all results, positive and negative, deserve rethinking: some need full articles, while others suit blogs, preprints or post-publication review. Mike asks about interest from people automating research with AI. Stefan says computer scientists and AI researchers are contacting him because garbage in means garbage out, and better data includes failures. Mike thanks Stefan for joining and wishes the journal success.
